text: Everything from the SIEM to the correlation rules exists to produce one thing: an alert landing in a queue in front of a Tier 1 analyst. What happens next is the real job, and it runs the same way every time -- an alert fires, the analyst reviews it, classifies it, and takes an initial action. That loop runs dozens or hundreds of times a shift.

Review means pulling up the underlying event, the host or account involved, and whatever context the SIEM surfaces alongside it -- not just reading the alert's label. Classification sorts the alert into one of three outcomes. And the initial action, closing it, escalating it, or starting containment, depends entirely on getting that classification right.

New analysts assume triage has two outcomes, real or fake, but it has three. A true positive is malicious activity that really happened. A false positive is simply wrong -- the activity didn't happen as described. A benign true positive is the one people miss: the alert is accurate, the activity really happened, but it's legitimate -- an admin logging in while traveling, confirmed by an IT ticket, versus that same login pattern at 3am followed by a failed attempt to add an MFA device.

Triage speed and accuracy both matter, and failing at either one is costly. Every alert sitting untouched in a queue gives a real attacker more dwell time -- more hours operating undetected. But rushing and waving off alerts without checking the data misses genuine incidents, and escalating everything "just in case" burns Tier 2's time and trains the team to ignore escalations.

Both failure modes trace back to the same mistake: skipping the review step and guessing instead of checking what the data actually shows. Next, Lesson 18 covers what that checking actually looks like -- validating an alert against its underlying data, scoping how far an incident has spread, and deciding when it genuinely needs to go to Tier 2.
